claim: WA is NOT the cut-off state the WA community assumes: it reached 117 of 119 species. TAS has that problem, with 74 of 119 never once buyable there. The hard-to-find badge must share the dataset's denominator.

body.window: 189 measurable days of 197, 8 excluded as scraper outages, 27 nurseries, 119 species
body.national_saturation: 100 of 119 species in stock somewhere every measured day. National rarity is largely resolved; the finding is STATE reachability, not species.
body.wa_correction: WA is NOT the cut-off state despite what the WA rare fruit community assumes; quarantine costs it ~7% of breadth and it reached 117 of 119 species. TAS has the problem WA thinks it has: 74 of 119 never once buyable there.

hard_to_find_badge.fixed: 2026-09-17, DEC-341. The availability half averaged over LISTINGS, so one nursery's twenty dead variety SKUs outvoted four nurseries carrying one each. 37 species lost the badge; 24 of them had been in stock somewhere every one of the 189 measured days while the site called them hard to find.
hard_to_find_badge.guarantee: badge and the CC BY dataset now share one rollup and one denominator; agreement asserted over all 119 species by tests/test_rarity_scores.py
hard_to_find_badge.do_not: do not move HARD_TO_FIND_SCORE (65) to change the badge count; nursery scarcity alone caps at 60, so the threshold is what keeps the claim honest

method_caveats: availability.json records NO day entry for a delisted product: absence != out of stock.
Bare-root seasonality is not scarcity; some listings are seed packets, not trees.
The panel grew from 8 on day one to 27, so early days undercount. The old '19 to 27' claim was wrong and was repeated internally for two months.
